segments.title: The Fog and the Labyrinth: Opening Chancery

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close reading of one of the greatest novels in the English language.

I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be moving through Dickens' masterpiece chapter by chapter — the fog, the labyrinth, the characters who haunt you long after you've closed the book.
Today we begin at the beginning: the Court of Chancery, the fog that opens the novel, and the world Dickens conjured to contain them both.
Joining me are three extraordinary guides to this novel, and I want to introduce each of them properly.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more Dickens audiobooks than any living performer — he knows every sentence of this novel in his bones, and he hears things in the prose that most readers simply miss.
Oliver, welcome.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian whose specialty is Victorian institutions — which means Chancery is, for him, almost personal territory.
James brings the history — what these courts actually were, who they actually destroyed.
James, glad you're here.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times since — which tells you everything about the hold this novel takes.
Caroline reads for the experience — what moves, what delights, what makes you stop mid-sentence and read it again.
Caroline, wonderful to have you.
Now — let's talk about the opening of Bleak House, and what Dickens does before we've even met a single character.
Oliver, you've read this opening more times than most people have read it once — where does it take you?
Every time — every single time — I open my mouth on that first paragraph, something happens in my chest.
It's the fog, obviously — Dickens just keeps piling it on, fog upon fog, mud upon mud — but it's also something underneath the fog.
There's a fury there, barely contained by the prose.
And then Chancery enters, and Dickens does something I adore — he gives us a judge defending the court, right to your face.
The setup is this:
"the Court of Chancery, though the shining subject of much popular prejudice, was almost immaculate."
"Almost immaculate." Two of the greatest words Dickens ever placed side by side.
The judge doesn't say "perfect" — he can't quite manage that — so he lands on "almost immaculate" and expects us to be grateful.
What makes that passage so precise is that it's not really a caricature — or not only a caricature.
Chancery judges in the 1840s and early 1850s actually did make arguments of this kind — that the court's delays were the public's own fault for not funding more judicial appointments.
The real Court of Chancery had a backlog stretching decades — decades — and the institutional response was essentially what Dickens describes.
The blame was always transferred — to the public, to underfunding, to ancient precedent reaching back, as Dickens notes with beautiful disdain, to Richard the Second.
And then Dickens adds that magnificent parenthesis:
"I believe by Richard the Second, but any other king will do as well."
That throwaway line is devastating — it says that the court's origins are so obscure, so anciently self-justifying, that the founding monarch is essentially interchangeable.
What I keep coming back to, reading that passage, is the parenthesis about the judge's eye.
Dickens puts himself in the room — he's one of a hundred and fifty people being told the court is almost immaculate — and then:
"at which point I thought the judge's eye had a cast in my direction."
He's been spotted as the sceptic in the room, and he knows it, and he wants us to know it.
It's funny, but it's also Dickens staking his position — he's not going to pretend.
That's exactly right — and it sets up something Esther does from the other direction entirely.
Because we have two narrators in this novel, and they couldn't be less alike in how they see the world.
The omniscient narrator attacks — that's the word, attacks — the institutions with almost theatrical rage.
And then Esther wakes before dawn and watches the mist lift, and she says something so quietly beautiful it stops you cold.
"As the prospect gradually revealed itself and disclosed the scene over which the wind had wandered in the dark, like my memory over my life."
"Like my memory over my life" — she doesn't explain it, she doesn't push it, she just lets it sit there.
That is a character who has had to piece herself together in the dark.
She does that all the way through — offers these huge emotional admissions wrapped in the quietest possible language.
And notice what she does at the end of that passage — the Abbey Church throws a softer shadow than you'd expect from its rugged character, and Esther says:
"But so from rough outsides, serene and gentle influences often proceed."
She's describing the church — but she's also describing herself, or hoping to.
"I hope I have learnt" — that little parenthesis is heartbreaking if you know what's coming for her.
The contrast between the two narrators also does something structurally important that I think is easy to underestimate.
The omniscient narrator gives us institutions and systems — Chancery, the fog as social metaphor, England as a machine of organized neglect.
Esther gives us individuals — specific faces, specific suffering.
And when those two registers meet — when a character from Esther's narrative falls into the machinery of the omniscient world — the effect is annihilating.
Which brings us to Mrs. Pardiggle's visit, and that cottage, and what Esther sees inside it.
"Besides ourselves, there were in this damp, offensive room a woman with a black eye, nursing a poor little gasping baby by the fire."
Dickens doesn't editorialize — he just lists.
The woman, the man on the ground, the young man with the dog, the bold girl washing in dirty water.
And the detail that undoes me every time: the woman turns her face toward the fire to hide her bruised eye from the visitors.
She is ashamed — not her abuser, but her — and nobody in the room seems to notice that this is the indictment.
And "nobody gave us any welcome" — that's the last line of that passage.
Mrs. Pardiggle has marched in with great moral determination, as Dickens says, and these exhausted, suffering people simply look up and then look away.
They are not grateful for her charity — they have no reason to be.
Esther notices it, and Esther winces — but Pardiggle barrels on.
That contrast between genuine feeling and performed virtue is one of the things Bleak House does better than any novel I know.
We'll come back to Mrs. Pardiggle and what Dickens is doing with philanthropy in this novel — it's rich territory.
But first — the fog itself, and what it means that Dickens opens the entire novel not with a character or a scene, but with a weather condition that is also a moral condition.
We'll pick that up in our next segment — stay with us.

segments.title: Following the Thread: Lady Dedlock's Secret Unravels

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been circling the great labyrinth of Dickens' plot, and today we follow what is perhaps its most electrifying thread — Lady Dedlock's secret, and the man who holds the end of it.
With me, as ever, is Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has read more Dickens aloud than anyone breathing — who hears these scenes as performance first.
Professor James Blackstone, legal historian, who can tell us precisely what kind of machinery is grinding beneath the surface of all these polished drawing rooms.
And Caroline Woodcourt, critic and devoted re-reader, who came to this novel as a teenager and has never quite escaped it.
The chapter we're entering today is Chapter Twelve — and Dickens springs his trap with exquisite patience.
What strikes me every time — every single time I read this section — is the comedy Dickens hides inside the danger.
Sir Leicester unfolding that letter is one of the great comic set-pieces of the novel.
He fumbles with his eyeglass, he wanders into the wrong part of the letter — 'In the matter of the right of way — I beg your pardon, that's not the place' —
while his wife sits two feet away, knowing that her entire life may be about to collapse.
That is Dickens at his most controlled — the more Sir Leicester dawdles, the tighter the screw turns on Lady Dedlock.
And when it finally arrives, Tulkinghorn's message is almost offhand in its menace:
"I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him."
Three words at the end. Just three. Tulkinghorn could not be more dangerous if he tried.
That offhandedness is entirely characteristic, and it's worth understanding what it represents in institutional terms.
Tulkinghorn is a solicitor of the old school — not a barrister arguing in court, but a keeper of documents, wills, settlements, and above all, secrets.
Dickens understood that such men derived their power not from what they said, but from what they chose not to say — and when.
There's a passage that describes Tulkinghorn arriving at Chesney Wold that I think captures this perfectly:
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
And then Dickens goes further — 'Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret.'
We genuinely don't know whether Tulkinghorn is loyal to the Dedlocks or simply using them, and Dickens refuses to resolve that ambiguity.
He is his own client. That is terrifying precisely because it is true to the type.
What devastates me about this chapter is where Dickens places the camera, so to speak.
Sir Leicester gazes into the fire. The great ancestral face on the staircase, we're told — wholly indifferent, wholly elsewhere.
And the two people who hold each other's lives in their hands are performing perfect, glacial courtesy — inches apart.
Listen to how Dickens renders the standoff:
"During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another."
That phrase — 'customary deportment' — is doing so much work. They are not alarmed. They are not betraying anything. They are simply two professionals in a locked room.
And yet the sentence beneath — the one that asks what each would give to know how much the other knows — is among the finest Dickens ever wrote.
You have to read that sentence aloud to feel its full weight. May I?

"But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows—
all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
'For the time.' Those three words are doing exactly the same work as 'I have seen him.'
Dickens is telling us: the concealment is temporary. The revelation is coming. He just won't say when.
As a performer, that is the most exquisite kind of suspense — the kind where the audience already knows the trap is set.
And it continues, meeting after meeting, with no apparent change.
The passage describing their subsequent encounters at Chesney Wold has always struck me as almost unbearably compressed:
"They meet again at dinner—again, next day—again, for many days in succession."
That repetition — again, again, again — is weeks of tension collapsed into a single sentence.
And then we get those paired portraits — Lady Dedlock, 'the exhausted deity,' and Tulkinghorn, 'the speechless repository of noble confidences.'
What I find historically precise about that second phrase is that it was essentially a job description.
The great solicitors of the Victorian era were repositories — and Dickens knew that a repository is not necessarily an ally.
And then, entirely apart from all of this, there is Esther.
Dickens shifts us to a completely different register — out of the gothic chess match of Chesney Wold and into something rawer, stranger, more personal.
Esther encounters Lady Dedlock for the first time, and something in her simply — breaks open.
She describes it like this:

"There was something quickened within me, associated with the lonely days at my godmother's; yes, away even to the days when I had stood on tiptoe to dress myself at my little glass after dressing my doll."
She is absolutely certain she has never seen this woman before in her life. And yet.
That image of the little girl on tiptoe, dressing her doll — it's Dickens at his most precise about memory.
The body remembers what the mind cannot name.
What strikes me about that passage, coming at it from the performance side, is how much Dickens trusts Esther's confusion.
He doesn't rush to explain it. He lets her flounder — beautifully.
She tries a rational explanation — perhaps there is a resemblance to her godmother? — and then dismisses it, and you can hear her doing so:
"The stern decision which had worn into my godmother's face, like weather into rocks, was so completely wanting in the face before me."
'Like weather into rocks.' That simile deserves a round of applause on its own.
But then Esther arrives at the thing she cannot account for, the sentence that always stops me cold:

"I—I, little Esther Summerson, the child who lived a life apart and on whose birthday there was no rejoicing—seemed to arise before my own eyes, evoked out of the past by some power in this fashionable lady."
That repetition of 'I — I' — Dickens is showing us Esther stammering inwardly, reaching for herself and barely finding her footing.
There's a structural point worth making here, which is that Dickens is running two completely different epistemological systems simultaneously.
In the Tulkinghorn chapters, knowledge is power — it is legal, documentary, controlled.
Someone has a piece of paper; someone else wants to know who wrote it. It is knowable, in principle.
But Esther's knowledge is of an entirely different order — pre-verbal, somatic, beyond her own comprehension.
The secret is approaching her from outside the legal system entirely, through blood and memory and something she cannot name.
Dickens understood — and this is rather remarkable for 1852 — that some truths arrive through the body before they arrive in the mind.

That juxtaposition — the legal machinery grinding away in one half of the novel, and Esther's wordless, embodied recognition unfolding in the other — really is what makes this strand of the book so extraordinary.
The secret is both a document and a wound, and Dickens pursues it on both fronts at once.

Coming up, we'll follow what happens when Tulkinghorn's patience finally runs out — and ask what Dickens is really saying about power, knowledge, and whether any secret can survive long enough to matter.

segments.title: The Degradation of Richard: A Cautionary Descent

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great novel apart — slowly, carefully, and with enormous affection.
I'm your host, and today we turn to one of the novel's most quietly devastating arcs: the deterioration of Richard Carstone.
Richard is young, charming, genuinely loveable — and Dickens destroys him with patient, almost surgical precision.
With me today are three people who know this novel as well as anyone alive.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more Dickens audiobooks than any performer living — he hears the rhythms of this prose the way a musician hears a score.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who knows exactly what Chancery was, what it did to people, and what Dickens understood about it that his contemporaries preferred to ignore.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read Bleak House five times and still finds new things to love — and to mourn — in its pages.
Let's begin with the early warning signs — the passages in Chapter Seventeen where Richard tells Esther, in his own words, what is wrong with him.
What strikes me every time I read Chapter Seventeen is how completely Richard diagnoses himself — and how little it helps him.
He says it to Esther with this slightly rueful charm, as though the confession itself might substitute for the reform.
And the passage that stops me every time begins when he says, quite openly —

"I seem to want something or other to stand by. Even you have no idea how fond I am of Ada — my darling cousin, I love you, so much! — but I don't settle down to constancy in other things. It's such uphill work, and it takes such a time!"
That exclamation — "I love you, so much!" — dropped into the middle of a confession of failure.
It's not an evasion exactly — the love is real — but it functions as one.
Richard pivots from admitting his inconstancy directly into the one thing he is constant about — and that pivot becomes the whole shape of his life.
And Dickens gives him that bracketed aside — "my darling cousin, I love you, so much!" — as pure stage direction.
When you read it aloud, you have to make a choice: is that tender, or is it a little desperate?
I've always played it as both simultaneously — which is how Dickens writes Richard throughout.
"It's such uphill work, and it takes such a time!" — there's something almost comic in the rhythm of that.
It sounds like a schoolboy complaining about Latin prep.
But the joke is doing terrible work — because what Richard finds "such uphill work" is simply the act of growing up.
Dickens is too good a comedian to separate the funny from the tragic, and Richard is his proof.
What Caroline and Oliver are identifying is the peculiar Chancery psychology — and Dickens understood it with something close to clinical precision.
The real Court of Chancery produced exactly this phenomenon: litigants who could not commit to anything else because the suit had colonised their imaginations entirely.
And what is so precise about Richard's plan to enter Kenge's office is that it sounds reasonable — it sounds like a solution.
He tells Esther —
"If I went into Kenge's office... I should have my eye on the — hum! — the forbidden ground — and should be able to study it, and master it."
That "hum!" is the tell.
He can't quite say "the suit" — he euphemises it as "forbidden ground," which is precisely how obsession works: you circle the thing you cannot name directly.
The Chancery records are full of men like Richard — not stupid men, often talented men — who persuaded themselves they were pursuing justice while the court quietly consumed them.
And Esther sees it — she sees it before Richard does, before almost anyone does.
There's a moment in Chapter Seventeen that I find extraordinarily poignant — where she watches Jarndyce watching Ada and Richard, and something shifts.
Dickens writes —
"This was the first time I ever saw him follow Ada with his eyes with something of a shadow on their benevolent expression."
"Something of a shadow" — that qualification is everything.
Dickens doesn't say grief, or foreboding, or jealousy — all of which are in there somewhere.
He says shadow — which is both more vague and more accurate than any of those words would be.
James will correct me if I'm wrong, but I think that shadow is Jarndyce knowing — already knowing — that the suit is going to take Richard.
He's watched it happen to people before.
And what you feel reading Chapter Twenty-Three, when Esther watches Richard haunting the court and befriending Miss Flite — that's when it becomes undeniable.
The language Dickens uses there is the language of doom.
He writes —
"What a fatal link was riveting between his fresh youth and her faded age, between his free hopes and her caged birds, and her hungry garret, and her wandering mind."
"Riveting" — as in hammered into iron, permanent, inescapable.
And the triple repetition of "her" — her faded age, her caged birds, her wandering mind — that's a funeral bell tolling three times.
And Miss Flite is not incidental to that image — she is its entire point.
She is Richard's future, made visible and named, walking around the court in a bonnet.
The real Chancery cases — and I've read a good many of them — produced this precise progression: charm, hope, misdirected energy, debt, obsession, ruin.
What Dickens does that the court records cannot is give us the interiority — the way the sufferer cooperates in his own destruction while believing he is fighting it.
Richard tells himself he is studying law in order to protect Ada's interests.
He is doing the opposite of that — and the gap between his self-narration and reality is where the tragedy lives.
Which is why the confession in Chapter Twenty-Three hits so hard — because by then we know, even as Richard speaks, that the words won't hold.
He walks with Esther and says, with complete sincerity —

"I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow... If I were a more constant sort of fellow, I should have held on either to Badger or to Kenge and Carboy like grim death, and should have begun to be steady and systematic by this time, and shouldn't be in debt, and —"
He trails off.
That dash at the end of his sentence is Dickens refusing to complete it for him — because Richard cannot complete it for himself.
He knows what comes after "and —" but he cannot say it, and so neither can the novel.
I find that formally devastating.
"Like grim death" — you have to love that.
Richard uses the most energetic phrase in the language to describe how constant he wishes he had been — and the energy of the phrase itself is the problem.
He feels everything at full intensity.
The problem is that nothing sustains — each new enthusiasm arrives at full volume and fades almost immediately.
Except the suit — which never quite fades, which feeds on his frustrated energy rather than being diminished by it.
The repetition of "constant" in that passage — "constant sort of fellow," twice — is doing something, isn't it.
He's trying, by saying the word, to conjure the thing.
And what's quietly brilliant in these passages, taken together, is that Dickens never lets us feel superior to Richard — only sorrowful on his behalf.
He's too charming, too self-aware in his failures, too genuinely in love with Ada to be merely a cautionary figure.
In our next segment, we'll follow that deterioration further — into the darker chapters where Richard's obsession with Chancery begins to corrode something more than just his career.

segments.title: Street Crossing and Social Ruin: Jo's Testimony

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great novel apart — scene by scene, sentence by sentence — to ask why it still matters.
I'm your host, and today we're deep in the world of Jo — the crossing-sweeper — and the political class that doesn't know he exists.
With me are three people who have spent serious time with this novel and have strong feelings about it.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more Dickens audiobooks than any living person, and he hears this prose the way a conductor hears a score — every rhythm, every rest.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian of the Victorian period, and he knows exactly what kind of world produced Jo — and what it did to him.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has never quite recovered — which she counts as a compliment.
We're beginning with Jo's grief — those extraordinary scenes at the churchyard — and then we'll turn to the Boodle-Doodle-Noodle passage, which is Dickens being furiously funny.
Oliver, let's start with you — because the language in these scenes is doing something very unusual.
Yes — and what it's doing is almost unbearable if you let it land properly.
Jo has just seen the man who was kind to him laid out dead, and Dickens gives him this one small sentence to say it all.
"He wos wery good to me, he wos!"
That repetition at the end — "he wos" — that's not a grammatical tic, that's a heartbeat.
Dickens writes Jo's dialect not to mock him, but to make you hear him — really hear him — as a distinct human voice.
And then there's the detail of wiping his eyes with his "wretched sleeve" — that word, wretched, belongs to the narrator, not to Jo.
Dickens slips in the judgment so quietly you almost miss it.
And what follows that moment — the graveyard scene at night — is even quieter, and stranger, and more devastating.
Dickens stops calling Jo by name.
He becomes "a slouching figure" — then just "it."
"With the night comes a slouching figure through the tunnel-court to the outside of the iron gate.
It holds the gate with its hands and looks in between the bars, stands looking in for a little while."
That pronoun — "it" — is doing two things at once.
It shows us how society sees Jo — as a thing, not a person.
But it also — and this is the cruelty of the irony — gives the scene a kind of ghostly, mythic weight.
That dehumanising grammar is historically precise, whether Dickens intended it as such or not.
In the administrative language of the period — Poor Law reports, parish records — the destitute poor were routinely referred to in exactly that register.
They were cases, not people.
And then what Jo does next — the sweeping — is one of Dickens' most precisely observed gestures of devotion.
Dickens writes that Jo sweeps the step and the archway, and the word he chooses is "softly."
"It then, with an old broom it carries, softly sweeps the step and makes the archway clean."
He has nothing to give but his labour — and he gives it with tenderness.
The state has no mechanism to record that.
"Busily and trimly" — those two words together.
There's almost a comic energy to them — they're the words you'd use for a good housemaid or a diligent clerk.
But applied to Jo, sweeping a pauper's grave in the dark, they become — I don't know — almost unbearably poignant.
Dickens understood that the most devastating effects come from exactly this kind of tonal mismatch.
And then he just — departs.
No ceremony, no acknowledgment, no one watching.
That is Jo's entire existence in this novel, in miniature.
And Dickens cuts directly from that graveyard — from Jo's silent, invisible act of love — to Chesney Wold, to Lord Boodle explaining why the country is going to ruin.
James, you've written about what Chancery and Parliament actually meant in practice — how does the Boodle passage read to you?
It reads as a document.
The names are invented, obviously — Boodle, Doodle, Foodle — but the system they describe is perfectly accurate.
Cabinet formation in mid-Victorian England was almost entirely a matter of managing the expectations of a small circle of aristocratic families.
Dickens' joke is that the names are interchangeable — and the joke is that in practice, so were the men.
But what strikes me is the framing — Dickens lets Lord Boodle deliver his catastrophist rhetoric with complete sincerity.
"What follows? That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces — because you can't provide for Noodle!"
The country is shipwrecked — not because of Jo, mind, not because a child is sweeping a pauper's grave in the dark — but because Noodle has no portfolio.
The escalating rhyme scheme of the names is a gift — Coodle, Doodle, Foodle, Goodle, Hoodle, Joodle.
Reading it aloud, you feel yourself being pulled into a kind of dizzy momentum, like a music-hall patter song.
And then at the end: Quoodle.
Quoodle is so manifestly absurd that it punctures everything — and that's exactly the point.
By the time you reach Noodle's dilemma, the satire has already done its work — the whole edifice is seen to be ridiculous.
What I keep thinking about is the juxtaposition Dickens is making — perhaps not consciously, but structurally.
We've just left Jo at the gate — alone, unnamed, sweeping in the dark for love of a dead man.
And now we're with men who can't be named without a rhyme scheme, arguing about which office suits Noodle.
Jo's name is too simple to be said properly; Noodle's name is too absurd to be taken seriously.
And the novel holds them in the same chapter, the same breath, because that's what the world is.
That's the structural argument of the whole novel, really, isn't it — that these two worlds are not separate, but causally connected.
The Noodles govern, or fail to, and Jo sweeps a step in the dark.
Coming up, we'll look at what happens when those worlds collide — and what Dickens asks us to feel when they do.

segments.title: Comic Interludes in Darkness: The Ridiculous and the Sublime

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked — the show that takes Dickens seriously, which mostly means taking his jokes seriously.
Today's segment is about something that goes to the heart of what makes this novel so extraordinary — the way Dickens holds comedy and devastation in the same hand.
We're starting at the very beginning — that famous opening — and then letting ourselves loose on some of the novel's most delicious grotesques.
With me today: Oliver Trevelyan, who has read more Dickens aloud than any living soul and approaches the prose as a performer first.
Professor James Blackstone, legal historian, who knows exactly what was really going on inside the Court of Chancery — and has strong feelings about it.
And Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and devoted re-reader of Bleak House, who has spent a considerable portion of her life in Dickens' London.
Caroline — let's begin where the novel begins: that opening paragraph, London in November, and one of the most audacious first sentences in all of English literature.
Every time I return to that first page, I'm struck by something I can only describe as the nerve of it.
Dickens doesn't ease you in. He drops you into the mud — quite literally.
The sentences aren't even complete sentences, at first. "London. Michaelmas term lately over." It's almost telegraphic — as if the fog has got inside the grammar itself.
And then he does this extraordinary thing — he sets up the quote I want to read.

"As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill."
A dinosaur. Waddling. Up Holborn Hill.
That is not a simile you expect in an opening paragraph about legal corruption and social misery.
And yet it's absolutely right. The fog is primordial. The city is prehistoric. The whole thing is geological in its weight.
And it's funny. That's the thing people sometimes forget when they're busy being impressed by it.
The Megalosaurus is a joke. A brilliant, disorienting, slightly mad joke.
When I read that aloud — and I've read it, I dread to think, perhaps two hundred times now — the audience always laughs, and then feels faintly guilty about it.
Which is exactly the right response. Because Dickens is laughing too — and he's furious, simultaneously.
That double register — comic and indignant — is something he sustains for nine hundred pages. I don't know how he does it.
There's something quite precise happening in that opening, beyond the obvious comic exuberance.
The mud is doing real historical work. London in 1852 was genuinely, dangerously filthy — and the connection between physical filth and institutional rot was not metaphorical for Dickens.
The Thames was an open sewer. Cholera epidemics were a living memory. The fog was coal smoke. This was not atmosphere — it was a documentary record.
Which makes the joke more pointed, not less. The Megalosaurus isn't just surreal — it says: this city has evolved backwards.
That's exactly it — "evolved backwards." And then he does the sun mourning its own death. "Gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of the sun."
That line gets me every time. It's gothic and it's almost camp, and somehow it's both at once.
The whole opening is like that — pulling you between laughter and something much colder.
Oliver, I want to bring you to the Miss Flite scene — because she's another example of this, isn't she? The comedy and the tragedy arriving in the same breath.
There's a passage in Chapter Three where she addresses Esther and Richard, and it's one of the most quietly devastating things in the book.
Miss Flite. Oh, she's a masterpiece of compression.
On the surface she's a comic figure — small, fluttery, slightly unhinged, curtsying between sentences.
But then she turns to Richard, who has called her mad, and she says — let me get the rhythm right here, because the rhythm is everything —
"I was a ward myself. I was not mad at that time. I had youth and hope. I believe, beauty. It matters very little now."
Those little full stops. Each one a small door slamming.
And then she continues, and the comedy returns — but now it cuts differently. She sets up the quote for what follows —
"I have the honour to attend court regularly. With my documents. I expect a judgment. Shortly. On the Day of Judgment."
The joke is perfect. And it's appalling. Both things are completely true simultaneously.
What Miss Flite understands — in her madness, or rather through it — is that Chancery operates on an eschatological timescale.
The joke about the Day of Judgment is not really a joke. Cases in Chancery could run for generations. Jarndyce and Jarndyce itself was based on real cases Dickens knew about.
There was one case — the Thellusson case — that ran for sixty-two years and consumed virtually the entire estate it was supposed to protect.
Miss Flite has simply seen the system clearly — and the system looks, from the inside, exactly like what she describes.
What breaks my heart about Miss Flite is that detail — "I believe, beauty."
The "I believe" — she's not even certain. She's trying to remember herself. Trying to find the person who walked into that court room.
And then: "It matters very little now." Four words. The novel could stop there and we would understand everything about Chancery that Dickens wants us to understand.
And yet the scene is also funny. She curtsies after every sentence. That's a stage direction, essentially — Dickens is telling you exactly how to play her.
I've played her — well, voiced her — and the trap is to play her as purely pitiable. But she has a great deal of dignity. She knows more than anyone in that room.
Now — Boythorn. If Miss Flite is comedy edged with tragedy, Lawrence Boythorn might be comedy for its own glorious sake.
Oliver, his entrance in Chapter Nine is one of my favourite moments in the whole novel.
Boythorn arriving is one of the great theatrical entrances in all of Victorian fiction, and I will hear no argument on this point.
The household has waited for him all afternoon. Dinner has been put back an hour. The fire is the only light.
Dickens builds the anticipation with almost comic precision — and then the hall-door bursts open, and here it is —
"We have been misdirected, Jarndyce, by a most abandoned ruffian, who told us to take the turning to the right instead of to the left."
"He is the most intolerable scoundrel on the face of the earth. His father must have been a most consummate villain, ever to have such a son."
A man who entered a house for the first time, and his opening statement is a comprehensive denunciation of a stranger he met on a country road.
Dickens based him on Landor — the poet Walter Savage Landor — and apparently the portrait is not even exaggerated.
That's the most frightening thing about Boythorn. He might be real.
What I love is the escalation within that one speech. He starts with the man being a ruffian — which is strong enough.
Then he's the most intolerable scoundrel on the face of the earth — the entire earth, note — and then he reaches backwards in time to condemn the father.
All because someone gave him a wrong turning on a country road. Proportionality is not in Boythorn's vocabulary.
And yet — and this is the trick — Dickens makes us love him for it immediately. There's not a grain of real malice in him.
Boythorn is interesting to me because of his feud with Sir Leicester Dedlock — which is really a feud about property rights and right of way.
Dickens was serious about that. Right of way disputes were genuinely contentious in the 1850s, as common land was enclosed and the gentry extended their domains.
So Boythorn's explosive vehemence about a wrong turning is, in the wider novel, also a kind of principled resistance. He's a man who takes his rights seriously — all of them, extravagantly.
That's what I find when I perform him — there's no irony in Boythorn. He means every syllable. He would genuinely have had that man shot.
And somehow that sincerity is what makes him safe. The rage is completely transparent — and completely magnificent.
There's a pattern emerging, isn't there, across these three passages — the fog, Miss Flite, Boythorn.
Dickens never lets either register — the comic or the dark — sit still on its own. They're always in motion, always inflecting each other.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at the characters at the dark end of that spectrum — the real engines of cruelty in the novel, the ones who aren't funny at all.
We've spent this episode tracing some of Bleak House's darkest currents — secrets, suffering, and the long consequences that follow.
Before we close, I'd like to bring us back to one figure whose arc runs quietly beneath all of it: Richard Carstone.
Oliver, James, Caroline — we have three passages in front of us, and they tell a story that is almost unbearably poignant in retrospect.
Oliver, let's start with you — because Jarndyce's great speech to Richard in Chapter Thirteen is a speech that has to be performed, doesn't it?
It absolutely does, and it's one of those passages where you feel Dickens the performer standing directly behind Dickens the novelist.
Jarndyce doesn't lecture Richard. He rallies him. There's a tremendous urgency in the syntax.
Listen to how the passage opens — it practically bounces off the walls:
"Come! Now for our assumption. Now we lift our eyes up and look hopefully at the distance! Rick, the world is before you."
Three imperatives in rapid succession. He's trying to physically drag this young man forward by sheer force of affection.
And then the great central warning:
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
The heathen waggoner — that extraordinary flash of reference, almost throwaway, and then he's on to the next thing.
What strikes me every time I read that speech is how thoroughly Richard fails to hear it.
Jarndyce is giving him the entire moral grammar of the novel in one concentrated address.
"Constancy in love is a good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy in every kind of effort."
That is the thesis of Richard's story — stated plainly, early, while there's still time.
And what's devastating is that Jarndyce means every word with absolute tenderness. He's not scolding. He loves this boy.
Which makes the speech, on re-reading, almost unbearable. Because you know what comes next.
I'd like to hold that word — constancy — for a moment, because it does an enormous amount of work in the Victorian moral economy.
To the Victorian mind, inconstancy wasn't merely a character flaw. It was a form of social disorder.
A young man who could not settle to a profession was, in the eyes of his society, already partway to ruin.
Richard's tragedy isn't just personal. Chancery has given him a socially sanctioned excuse for exactly that inconstancy.
The suit becomes his alibi. Why apply yourself, when the case might at any moment render effort irrelevant?
Jarndyce sees this with perfect clarity. That final line of the speech is almost a legal ultimatum:
"If you entertain the supposition that any real success ever was or could be wrested from Fortune by fits and starts, leave that wrong idea here — or leave your cousin Ada here."
He stakes Ada against the delusion. It is a remarkably hard thing to say, for a gentle man.
And then — and this is what Dickens does, just when you think the weight of the argument might crush you — he gives us the image.
Richard and Ada leaving through those sunlit rooms. Esther watching them go.
It's one of the most quietly devastating passages in the whole novel, and it arrives without fanfare:
"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come."
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone."
"It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
The room darkened as they went out. I've read that line perhaps a hundred times. It never gets any easier.
What Dickens is doing there is almost cinematic, in a way that shouldn't be possible in 1852.
He's staging it — the long corridor, the figures receding, the light itself responding to their departure.
And Esther is at the window. She sees it and reports it with perfect simplicity. No editorialising.
The sunlight doesn't stand for hope allegorically. It IS hope. And then it's gone.
Which brings me to Chapter Seventeen, and that small, heartbreaking exchange where Esther appeals to Richard through Ada.
She knows she can't reach him directly. So she finds the one door still open — his love for Ada.
She says it was a part of his affectionate consideration for Ada —
"not to slight the importance of a step that might influence both their lives."
And it works — briefly. It makes him almost grave.
That word — almost. Dickens puts the whole tragedy in that one qualifier.
Caroline is right to isolate that word. Almost grave is not grave. The threshold is approached, and not crossed.
And what I find historically significant is who is doing the moral work in these scenes.
Jarndyce. Esther. Ada — by proxy. The women and the guardian. Never Richard's peers. Never his institutions.
The law, the army, the professions — the structures that were supposed to form young men of his class — they are precisely what destroys him.
Dickens is making a structural argument, not merely a moral one. Richard isn't weak. He's trapped.
The private love of three people is the only force that comes close to saving him. And it isn't quite enough.
James, that's the thing that makes Bleak House so extraordinary as a novel rather than just a great story.
Every individual failure is also a systemic indictment. Dickens manages to hold both simultaneously without losing either.
You grieve for Richard as a person. And then you look up and you see the machine that ground him down.
And the extraordinary thing — the thing that keeps me going back — is that even while all this darkness accumulates, the prose remains gloriously alive.
He never lets the indignation kill the joy of the telling. That is the genius of the thing.
That feels like exactly the right note on which to close this episode — the genius of the thing, held in tension with everything it costs.
Oliver Trevelyan, James Blackstone, Caroline Woodcourt — thank you all for a conversation that has been, in every sense, worthy of the novel.
Bleak House Unpacked will return, and there is so much more of this extraordinary novel still to explore.
Until then — keep reading, keep re-reading, and remember that the sun, as Dickens tells us, can cloud over very quickly.
